newsitem.title: USA: U.S. producer prices tumble in April.
newsitem.headline: U.S. producer prices tumble in April.

text.p: Producer prices posted their biggest decline in nearly four years in April, tumbling by 0.6 percent as food and energy costs declined, the Labour Department said on Wednesday.

It was the fourth straight month that producer prices have fallen and followed a 0.1 percent decline in March. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, producer prices fell by 0.1 percent in April, after a 0.4 percent rise in March.

The steep drop in producer prices in April should temper concerns on Wall Street that the inflation-wary Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at a meeting next Tuesday, but the decline was unlikely to extinguish those fears completely.
"It's obviously very good news," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Asked if the report would make the Federal Reserve less likely to raise interest rates next week, Liro said, "On the margin, yes, but I still think they're going to go.
"I don't think it's the on-the-ground inflation news that they're reacting to."
Wall Street analysts had expected producer prices to hold steady in May. Excluding food and energy costs, producer prices had been expected to post a 0.1 percent gain.

"It's certainly better than what investors had anticipated. But a lot of good news has already been factored in," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"We've yet to see any price pressures on the wholesale level. It will have to enter into discussions at the Fed."

The bond market reacted positively to the news, sending the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond up 14/32, or $4.375 per $1,000 of face value. The bond's yield, which moves in opposite direction to the price, fell to 6.89 percent from 6.93 percent Tuesday.
The stock market was also expected to rise following the producer price report.
"It's a very friendly number to the bonds and, of course, bonds are the gatekeeper to the stocks," said Larry Wachtel, chief analyst at Prudential Securities
The April drop in producer prices was widespread.
Energy prices continued their recent decline, falling by an additional 2.6 percent in April, led by weaker gasoline prices.

After surging in March, food prices also dropped in April. Vegetable prices plunged more than 20 percent, while fruit prices fell nearly 5 percent. The recent steep rise in coffee prices slowed, with prices increasing by nearly 5 percent in April after a gain of almost 13 percent in March.
Prices for a variety of items outside the volatile food and energy sectors also declined in April.
Car prices dropped by 0.5 percent, computer prices by 4.1 percent and civilian aircraft prices by 2 percent.
Tobacco prices, which rose 2.5 percent in March, increased 0.9 percent in April.
The producer price report also showed that there is little in the way of inflation in the pipeline.

Prices of intermediate goods, those items used to make the finished products that comprise the producer price index, fell by 0.3 percent in April. Prices of crude goods, materials at the start of the production process, dropped by 0.9 percent last month.
